divide.name: Statements and quantifiers
divide.brief: This part covers the logical language that later definitions are written in: statements and the connectives and, or, not; implication, including when 'if P then Q' is true (vacuous truth), the phrases 'necessary' and 'sufficient', and 'if and only if'; converse and contrapositive, and why only the contrapositive is equivalent; negating and, or and implication (De Morgan's laws, and 'not (P implies Q)' as 'P and not Q'). Then the quantifiers 'for all' and 'there exists' with their domain, translating between English mathematical sentences and quantified form, nested quantifiers and why their order matters ('for every x there is a y' against 'there is a y for every x'), and negating nested quantified statements mechanically by flipping each quantifier and negating the inner statement. Truth tables are used only as a quick check, not as a formal system. Edges: no proof methods here; how to prove a statement of each form belongs to 'Proof methods and proof writing'. Set notation such as 'x in A' is used informally as in school; sets are studied in 'Sets, functions and countability'. No epsilon definitions yet, but exercises should practise quantifiers on simple number statements of the same shape as later definitions (for example 'there is an M such that for all n, a_n <= M', 'for every n there is m > n with ...', and what it means for each to fail). What matters for this learner: fluency with nested quantifiers and their negation, so that later they can state on their own what 'does not converge', 'is not bounded' or 'is not continuous' means. This is the most important skill in the foundations and deserves many short exercises.

divide.name: Proof methods and proof writing
divide.brief: This part covers what a proof is and how to find and write one: reading a proof line by line, the structure of a statement deciding the structure of its proof, direct proof, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction (with the irrationality of sqrt 2 or the infinitude of primes as classic examples), proof by cases, proving 'if and only if' in both directions, disproving a universal statement with a counterexample, existence proofs (constructive, by exhibiting the object) and uniqueness proofs (assume two and show they are equal), and proving nested quantified statements: take the 'for all' variable arbitrary, then build the 'there exists' object, which may depend on it. This last template is what every epsilon proof later follows and should be stressed. Mathematical induction and strong induction (the well-ordering principle may be mentioned), with examples such as sum formulas, 2^n > n and Bernoulli's inequality. Proof writing: separating scratch work (working backwards, trying cases) from the final write-up, which runs forwards; conventions such as introducing every variable ('Let ...'), writing in full sentences, saying which method is used, and common mistakes (assuming what is to be proved, proving the converse, checking examples instead of proving). Edges: the logic of statements, quantifiers and negation comes from 'Statements and quantifiers' and is used, not retaught. Examples stay within school arithmetic: integers, parity, divisibility, rational numbers and simple algebraic inequalities. Properties of the real numbers, absolute value, bounding techniques and supremum belong to 'The real numbers'. Element-chasing proofs about sets and functions belong to 'Sets, functions and countability'. What matters for this learner: being able to write clear, correct proofs on their own and to read others' proofs critically. Give room for practice in choosing a method and turning scratch work into a clean write-up.

divide.name: Sets, functions and countability
divide.brief: This part covers the set and function language used throughout analysis: sets, elements, subsets, set-builder notation, the empty set, equality of sets proved by double inclusion (element-chasing proofs), union, intersection, difference and complement, De Morgan's laws for sets, Cartesian products, and indexed families with arbitrary unions and intersections (for example the union of [1/n, 1] or the intersection of (-1/n, 1/n) over all n, which the topology part relies on). Functions: domain, codomain and range, image and preimage of a set and how each behaves under unions, intersections and complements (preimages preserve all of them, images only unions), injective, surjective and bijective functions, composition, and inverse functions (a function has an inverse exactly when it is bijective). Cardinality by bijections: finite, countable and uncountable sets; countability of N x N, the integers and the rationals; a countable union of countable sets is countable; Cantor's diagonal argument stated for infinite decimal or binary sequences. Cantor's theorem on power sets may be mentioned. Edges: the logic and proof methods come from 'Statements and quantifiers' and 'Proof methods and proof writing' and are used here, not retaught. The uncountability of the real numbers is proved in 'The real numbers' (via nested intervals); here the diagonal argument is given for sequences of digits, with the real-number details left to that part. Relations and equivalence relations are not needed and are left out. What matters for this learner: confident handling of images and preimages (used later for continuity and open sets), indexed unions and intersections (used in topology), and countability (used for the rationals, Thomae's function and the discontinuities of monotone functions). These are also where the learner writes their first proofs about abstract objects rather than numbers.
